zh.title: 面對恐懼：佛陀在《怖駭經》如何原地不逃、直到恐懼消退（MN 4）
zh.seo_title: 面對恐懼怎麼辦？佛陀《怖駭經》的方法：不逃避、原地面對（MN 4 原典）
zh.seo_description: 半夜獨處心裡發毛、打坐坐到心慌意亂只想逃，佛教原典怎麼教？巴利《怖駭經》(MN4) 記載佛陀成道前獨居可怕林間，親述自己也曾害怕，如何不逃避、恐懼來襲時維持當下姿勢原地面對直到它消退，並先清理招來恐懼的內在雜染。逐段依原文解說，非心靈雞湯。
zh.question: 害怕、恐懼的時候，佛教怎麼教人面對？
zh.definition: 半夜一個人在家，忽然一點聲響就讓心揪起來；打坐坐到一半，念頭開始編故事，越想越怕，坐立難安只想開燈逃出房間——這種怕到失控、身體先於理智反應的經驗，很多人都有。巴利《怖駭經》(MN 4) 講的正是這個。佛陀成道之前，獨自住在最令人毛骨悚然的林間，坦承自己也曾生起同樣的念頭：這裡真的很難獨自撐下去。他的方法不是等恐懼自己過去，也不是說服自己不怕，而是很具體的一件事：恐懼在行、住、坐、臥任何一個姿勢襲來時，就維持那個姿勢，不換、不逃，一直待到把它看透、驅除為止。

sections.heading: 《怖駭經》在講什麼：獨居林中，恐懼會把心帶走

quotes.lead: 婆羅門向佛陀描述獨居林野有多難熬：
佛陀坦承，成道之前他自己也曾這樣想：

paragraphs: 半夜一個人待在偏僻的地方，風吹草動都覺得毛骨悚然——這種感覺很多人都懂。《怖駭經》（Bhayabheravasutta，MN 4）開頭，婆羅門遮那索尼就把這種感受具體攤開給佛陀聽：偏遠的森林曠野住處「難以承受」，獨居難為，孤獨也難以安樂；對還沒得定的比丘來說，「諸林彷彿會把心帶走」。這不是誇飾，是任何試過獨自在陌生地方過夜、或初學打坐坐到心慌意亂的人都認得的感覺。
佛陀沒有一開口就說「我從不害怕」。他坦承，就在成道之前、自己還是尚未圓滿覺悟的菩薩時，心裡也生起過一模一樣的念頭——林野住處確實難以承受，獨居難為，諸林會把心帶走。這部經從承認恐懼真實存在開始，不是從一個天生無畏的英雄開始；他要教的方法，是在這個前提上長出來的。

sections.heading: 恐懼的根源在自己：招來恐懼的內在雜染

quotes.lead: 佛陀列出招來恐懼的十六種內在雜染：
其中直接對準恐懼本身的一項：

paragraphs: 恐懼常常讓人覺得是外面的東西在威脅自己——黑影、聲音、未知。但佛陀在真正走進黑暗之前，先做了一件事：把恐懼的來源攤開來檢查。他逐一列出十六種狀況——身、語、意行不清淨、活命不清淨、貪婪、心懷惡意、惛沉睡眠、掉舉、疑惑、自讚毀他、天生膽怯、渴求名利、懈怠、失念、心散亂、愚昧無慧——並說：帶著這些雜染而獨居林野的沙門婆羅門，正是因為這些垢染，才「招來」（avhāyanti）不善的恐懼與驚怖。恐懼在這裡不是純粹來自外境，而是被自己心裡的狀態召喚出來的。
第十四項特別對準恐懼本身：有些人「因恐懼嚇呆、天生膽怯」才受用可怕的林野住處，就因為這份僵怖膽怯而招來恐怖可畏。佛陀逐項檢視自己，確認並非膽怯之人、而是「毫無毛骨悚然之感」；每看見自身具足一項清淨的品質，就「更加安然地在林中安住」。換句話說，與其只在恐懼當下咬牙硬撐，不如先照顧好自己的心——清淨的戒行、安定與正念，本身就會讓恐懼少了可以攀附的地方。

sections.heading: 不逃避，反而主動走向恐懼

quotes.lead: 佛陀主動選在最陰森的夜晚，走進最可怕的地方：

paragraphs: 怕的時候，人的本能是躲——躲回有燈光的地方、躲回人多的地方、躲進被窩裡。佛陀的做法完全相反。他心想：我何不在那些「廣為人知、特別標記」的夜晚——月半的第十四、十五日與第八日，傳統上被認為最陰森的夜晚——到那些「令人恐懼、毛骨悚然」的園林祠堂、森林祠堂、樹木祠堂等住所去住住看，「或許我確實能（親自面對）那恐懼與驚怖」。
這和「祈求保佑」「轉念想開就好」是不同的路數。佛陀不是設法讓恐懼別出現，而是主動把自己放進最容易生起恐懼的時間與地點，好在恐懼真的來時，就地把它看個清楚、處理掉。這部經裡，面對恐懼的第一個動作是「走過去」，不是「繞開」。

sections.heading: 恐懼來的那一刻：看清它多半只是心的期待

quotes.lead: 一隻鹿、一隻孔雀、一陣風——恐懼常常只是這樣起頭的：

paragraphs: 很多人怕黑、怕獨處，怕的其實不是真的發生了什麼，而是那個「萬一有什麼」的念頭停不下來。佛陀住在那些可怕的地方時，實際發生的往往只是很平常的聲響：一隻鹿走過來，一隻孔雀弄落了樹枝，或一陣風攪動一堆落葉。但他說，那一刻心裡會立刻竄出一個念頭：「確實，那令人恐懼怖畏之物正在到來！」——恐懼常常不是猛獸真的撲來，是心先把一個中性的聲音，解讀成「可怕的東西來了」。
接著他做了關鍵的一次反省：「難道我確實只是一直住在『期待恐懼』之中嗎？」他發現自己是抱著等著害怕的心態在過日子（bhayapaṭikaṅkhī，期待恐懼）。於是他下定決心：「我何不就以本然的姿態——當那恐懼如實到來時，就用那樣的自己，如實地去面對、驅除它。」不再逃，也不再預先繃緊等著怕，恐懼以什麼樣子來，就以當下這個樣子的自己去承接。

sections.heading: 面對的方法：維持當下的姿勢，直到恐懼消退

quotes.lead: 恐懼在行走時來，他就維持走的姿勢：
站、坐、臥時來，也是同樣的原則：

paragraphs: 這是整部經最具體、也最能直接拿來用的方法。當恐懼在他「經行（來回走動）」時到來，他就不站起來、不坐下、也不躺下，一直維持著走的姿勢，直到把那恐懼驅除為止。恐懼在他「站著」時到來，他就不改去走、不坐、不躺，就站著把它驅除。坐著時、躺著時也一樣：恐懼在哪個姿勢裡找上他，他就用那個姿勢承接，絕不因為害怕而換姿勢、起身、或逃開。
人在害怕時的本能是動——起身、走開、蜷縮、逃跑；佛陀刻意不給恐懼這個滿足，就用它找上你時的那個姿勢原地不動地面對，直到它自己退去。恐懼被清楚地當成一個會來、也會走的現象來對待，而不是一個非服從不可的命令——這句話換成任何一個半夜心慌的人身上，都用得上。

sections.heading: 面對之後：心不是麻木，而是清明、能定、能覺

quotes.lead: 驅除恐懼之後，他的認知變得更如實：
心穩定下來之後，他依序證得：

paragraphs: 有人擔心，硬撐著不逃是不是會把自己逼到麻木、壓抑？經文給的答案不是。佛陀特別點出：有些沙門婆羅門「明明是夜晚，卻認知為白晝；明明是白晝，卻認知為夜晚」，他說那是住在迷惑之中；而他自己是「夜晚就如實認知為夜晚，白晝就如實認知為白晝」。面對恐懼的成果，是看得更清楚、更如實，不是自我催眠。
在這個基礎上，經文接著說：他的「精進已發起、不懈怠，正念已現前、無混亂，身體寂靜、不激動，心已集中於一境」。正是靠著這樣被安定下來的心，他依序進入初禪到第四禪，並在那一夜證得三明（宿命、天眼、漏盡），最終解脫。面對恐懼在這部經裡不是終點，而是把心穩住、讓整條修行道路得以展開的入口。

sections.heading: 覺悟之後為何仍住林中：現法樂住與悲憫後人

quotes.lead: 佛陀主動點破一個可能的誤會：

paragraphs: 經末，佛陀主動點破一個可能的誤會：有人也許會想，「沙門瞿曇至今想必仍未離貪、未離瞋、未離癡，所以才還住在那些偏遠的森林裡。」他明確否認：「此事不應如此看待。」對已經覺悟的人來說，住在林中早已不是被恐懼考驗，也不是還有未斷的煩惱。
他給出兩個理由：一是「自己的現法樂住」——當下就安樂地安住；二是「悲憫後世人眾」。當年那個在最可怕的夜晚原地面對恐懼的修行者，如今把同一片森林留成了一份現成的安樂，也留成一份給後人的示範。從這個角度看，這段第一人稱的面對恐懼實錄，本身就是那份「悲憫後人」的一部分——包括正在讀這段經文、正被恐懼困住的我們。

zh.mahayana_note: 《怖駭經》是佛陀成道前後的第一人稱實修敘事，與大乘教義沒有直接的義理關聯。不過「無畏／施無畏」（abhaya）這個主題，在後世佛教有豐富的發展：佛菩薩造像常見的「施無畏印」（abhaya-mudrā），以及觀世音菩薩被稱為「施無畏者」、於眾生怖畏急難中令得無畏，都把「面對恐懼」放進了祈請與他力護佑的脈絡，與 MN 4 這種第一人稱、靠自己原地訓練的路數是不同的側重。本頁僅呈現巴利經文中的用法與敘事，不對各系詮釋作評判。

faq.a: 怕到心跳加速、只想起身逃離的那一刻，《怖駭經》(MN 4) 教的方法有三層。一是先清理內心——經文指出膽怯、掉舉、疑惑等雜染會「招來」恐懼，所以清淨的戒行、安定與正念本身就會減少恐懼；二是不逃避，甚至主動走向會害怕的處境；三是恐懼真的來時，維持當下的行、住、坐、臥姿勢，不因害怕而改變或逃開，直到恐懼被驅除。這是靠自己原地訓練的路數，不是靠祈求外力或自我催眠。
《怖駭經》（Bhayabheravasutta，MN 4）標題直譯即「恐懼與驚怖之經」。婆羅門問佛陀：獨居森林那麼難熬，該怎麼辦？佛陀便親述自己成道前如何獨居可怕的林間：先檢視招來恐懼的十六種內在雜染，再刻意在最陰森的夜晚住進令人毛骨悚然的地方，當恐懼來襲時原地面對、直到它消退；恐懼被安頓後，心變得清明安定，於是入四禪、證三明而覺悟。最後他說明覺悟後仍住林中，是為了現法樂住與悲憫後人。

faq.q: 打坐或獨處時感到害怕，怎麼辦？
faq.a: 《怖駭經》給的提示很具體。第一，先認得恐懼常是心的「期待」在作用——佛陀在林中聽到鹿走、孔雀弄落樹枝、風吹落葉，心就立刻解讀成「可怕的東西來了」，他因此反省自己是不是一直「住在期待恐懼之中」。第二，不要一害怕就起身逃開；經文的做法是維持當下的姿勢，把恐懼當成一個會來也會走的現象，原地看著它退去。第三，日常培養正念與定，讓心先安定，恐懼就少了攀附之處。

faq.q: 恐懼來的時候，該換個姿勢或起身走動嗎？
faq.a: 《怖駭經》的答案很反直覺：不換。佛陀說，恐懼在他經行時到來，他就維持走的姿勢，不站、不坐、不躺，直到驅除它；在站、坐、臥時到來也一樣，一律用恐懼找上他的那個姿勢承接，絕不因害怕而改變姿勢或逃開。用意是不讓恐懼指揮身體——人害怕時的本能是動、是逃，而他刻意不給恐懼這個滿足，讓它在自己不動之中自然退去。
《怖駭經》裡佛陀坦承，成道之前他還是菩薩時，也曾覺得林野住處難以承受、諸林會把心帶走。他並沒有把自己描寫成天生無畏，而是描述了一段主動面對、逐步克服的訓練過程。經文同時指出，恐懼多半是被修行者自身的膽怯、掉舉、疑惑等雜染所招引；他逐項檢視、確認自己已離這些雜染，才更加安然地住在林中——面對恐懼因此既是當下的功夫，也是長期清淨內心的成果。

en.title: Facing Fear: How the Buddha Stood His Ground Until It Passed (MN 4)
en.seo_title: How to Face Fear? The Buddha's Method in the Fear and Dread Discourse (MN 4)
en.seo_description: How does early Buddhism teach facing fear? In the Pali Bhayabherava Sutta (MN 4), the Buddha recounts dwelling alone in the forest before awakening: he did not flee but held whatever posture he was in and faced fear (bhayabherava) until it subsided—and first cleared the inner defilements that invite fear.
en.question: When fear or dread arises, how does Buddhism teach us to face it?
en.definition: According to the Pali Bhayabherava Sutta (MN 4), before his awakening the Buddha dwelt alone in frightening forest places. He did not avoid fear but deliberately sought out the most hair-raising nights and dwellings; when fear arose while he was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he held that very posture—refusing to change it or flee—until he had dispelled the fear. The sutta also points out that fear is largely "invited" by the practitioner's own defilements (timidity, restlessness, doubt), so facing fear is at the same time a purifying of the mind.

sections.heading: What MN 4 is about: in the forest, fear can carry off the mind
paragraphs: The Pali title of the Bhayabherava Sutta (MN 4) translates literally as the "Discourse on Fear and Dread." It opens with the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi raising a very practical difficulty: remote forest and wilderness lodgings are hard to bear, solitude is hard to keep, and aloneness is hard to enjoy; for a monk who has not yet gained concentration, he says, "the forests seem to carry off the mind." This is exactly what many people feel alone at night, or when they first sit in meditation—not an abstract philosophical worry, but the body prickling and the mind scattering.

Notably, the Buddha does not begin by posing as someone who never felt fear. He admits that just before his full awakening, while still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this very thought had arisen in him too: forest lodgings are indeed hard to bear, solitude hard, and the forests seem to carry off the mind. In other words, the discourse does not start from a fearless hero but from acknowledging that fear is real and genuinely hard—and it is on that basis that the method of facing fear is developed.

sections.heading: The root of fear is in oneself: the defilements that invite it
paragraphs: Before actually walking into the dark, the Buddha does one thing first: he lays out the sources of fear for inspection. One by one he lists sixteen conditions—impure bodily, verbal, and mental conduct; impure livelihood; covetousness; ill will; sloth and torpor; restlessness; doubt; self-praise and disparaging others; being timid and fearful by nature; craving gain, honor, and fame; laziness; muddled mindfulness; an unconcentrated, wandering mind; and dull-witted stupidity—and says: ascetics and brahmins who resort to the forest carrying such defilements, precisely because of those defilements, "invite" (avhāyanti) unwholesome fear and dread. Here fear does not come purely from the environment; it is summoned by the state of the practitioner's own mind.

The item that bears most directly on fear itself is the fourteenth: some resort to frightening forest lodgings while "paralyzed by fear, timid by nature," and by that very cowering timidity they invite terror. The Buddha examines himself against each item and confirms he is not a timid person but "free of the horripilation of terror"; and each time he sees a pure quality in himself, he "dwells all the more at ease in the forest." This gives facing fear an often-overlooked premise: rather than merely gritting your teeth in the moment of fear, first tend to the mind—pure conduct, calm, and mindfulness themselves leave fear with less to grab onto.

sections.heading: Not avoiding it—deliberately walking toward fear
paragraphs: Then comes the turning point of the whole discourse. The Buddha did not try to avoid frightening situations; he deliberately went toward them. He thought: why not, on those nights "well known and specially marked"—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight, traditionally considered the eeriest nights—go and stay in those "frightening, hair-raising" garden shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines, thinking, "perhaps I might actually meet that fear and dread"?

This is very different from the "pray for protection from an outside power" or "just think positive" advice that fills the internet. The Buddha does not arrange for fear not to appear; he actively places himself in the time and place most likely to produce fear, so that when fear really comes he can look at it clearly, on the spot, and be done with it. In this discourse, the first move in facing fear is to walk over to it, not to walk around it.

sections.heading: The moment fear arrives: seeing that it is mostly the mind's anticipation
paragraphs: While staying in such places, what actually happened was usually something quite ordinary: a deer would come near, a peacock would knock down a twig, or the wind would stir a heap of leaves. But, the Buddha says, at that moment a thought would immediately shoot up: "Surely this is that fear and dread coming!" Fear is often not a beast actually lunging, but the mind first interpreting a neutral sound as "the frightening thing is here."

He then made a decisive reflection: "Am I really just dwelling in constant expectation of fear?" He noticed he was living in a stance of waiting-to-be-afraid (bhayapaṭikaṅkhī, expecting fear). So he resolved: "Why don't I—just as I am, when that fear and dread comes as it really is—subdue it in exactly that same state?" No more fleeing, and no more tensing up in advance to be scared; rather, in whatever form fear arrives, meet it as the person you are in that very moment.

sections.heading: The method: hold whatever posture you are in until fear subsides
paragraphs: What follows is strikingly concrete—and done with the body. When fear came while he was walking back and forth, he would not stand, sit, or lie down; he kept walking until he had dispelled it. When fear came while he was standing, he would not switch to walking, sitting, or lying down, but dispelled it standing. The same for sitting and for lying down: in whatever posture fear found him, he received it in that posture, never changing position, getting up, or fleeing because he was afraid.

This is the most counterintuitive—and most usable—move in the whole discourse: don't let fear command your body. The instinct when afraid is to move—to get up, walk off, curl up, run; and the Buddha deliberately denies fear that satisfaction, meeting it motionless in the very posture it caught him in, until it withdraws on its own. Fear is treated squarely as a phenomenon that comes and also goes, not as an order that must be obeyed.

sections.heading: After facing it: not numbness, but clarity, concentration, and awakening
paragraphs: Having dispelled fear, the Buddha's mind did not become dull or suppressed. He specifically notes that some ascetics and brahmins "perceive night as day and day as night," which he calls dwelling in delusion; whereas he himself "perceives night, when it is night, as night, and day, when it is day, as day." The fruit of facing fear is seeing more clearly and more truly—not self-hypnosis.

On that footing, the discourse continues: his "energy was aroused and unsluggish, mindfulness established and unconfused, the body tranquil and unagitated, the mind concentrated and one-pointed." It was precisely on such a steadied mind that he entered the first through the fourth jhāna and, over that night, realized the three true knowledges (recollection of past lives, the divine eye, the destruction of the taints), culminating in liberation. So in this sutta, facing fear is not the end point but the doorway that settles the mind and lets the whole path unfold.

sections.heading: Why he still dwelt in the forest after awakening: a pleasant abiding, and compassion for those to come
paragraphs: Near the end, the Buddha himself heads off a possible misunderstanding: someone might think, "The ascetic Gotama must still not be free of greed, hatred, and delusion, and that is why he goes on living in remote forests." He flatly rejects this: "It should not be regarded so." For one who is already awakened, dwelling in the forest is no longer a test by fear, nor a sign of undissolved defilement.

He gives two reasons: first, "a pleasant abiding here and now"—dwelling at ease in the present; and second, "compassion for later generations." The one who once stood his ground before fear on the eeriest of nights has now made that same forest into a ready-made ease—and into a demonstration left for those who come after. Seen this way, this first-person record of facing fear is itself part of that "compassion for later generations"—including us, reading these lines.

en.mahayana_note: The Bhayabherava Sutta is a first-person account of the Buddha's own practice around the time of his awakening, and it has no direct doctrinal link to Mahāyāna teaching. The theme of "fearlessness" (abhaya), however, developed richly in later Buddhism: the "gesture of fearlessness" (abhaya-mudrā) common in images of buddhas and bodhisattvas, and Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin) as the "giver of fearlessness" who grants freedom from fear to beings in peril, both set "facing fear" within a register of invocation and protective other-power—a different emphasis from MN 4's first-person, self-reliant training on the spot. This page presents only the usage and narrative found in the Pali text and does not adjudicate among the various interpretations.

faq.q: How does Buddhism teach us to face fear?
faq.a: Taking the Bhayabherava Sutta (MN 4) as an example, the Buddha's method has three levels. First, clear the mind beforehand—the sutta notes that timidity, restlessness, doubt, and other defilements "invite" fear, so pure conduct, calm, and mindfulness themselves reduce it. Second, do not avoid fear, and even move toward frightening situations on purpose. Third, when fear actually arrives, hold whatever posture you are in—walking, standing, sitting, or lying—without changing it or fleeing, until the fear is dispelled. This is a path of self-reliant training on the spot, not of praying to an outside power or self-hypnosis.

faq.q: What is the Bhayabherava Sutta about?
faq.a: The Bhayabherava Sutta (MN 4) translates literally as the "Discourse on Fear and Dread." A brahmin asks the Buddha how one copes with how hard forest solitude is. The Buddha recounts how, before his awakening, he dwelt alone in frightening forest places: first he examined the sixteen inner defilements that invite fear; then he deliberately stayed in hair-raising spots on the eeriest nights, facing fear on the spot when it came until it subsided. Once fear was settled, his mind grew clear and concentrated, and he entered the four jhānas and realized the three knowledges, awakening. Finally he explains that he still dwells in the forest for a pleasant abiding here and now and out of compassion for later generations.

faq.q: I feel afraid when meditating or alone—what should I do?
faq.a: MN 4 offers very concrete pointers. First, recognize that fear is often the mind's "anticipation" at work—in the forest the Buddha heard a deer walk, a peacock drop a twig, the wind stir leaves, and his mind instantly read it as "the frightening thing is here," which led him to ask whether he was constantly "dwelling in expectation of fear." Second, don't get up and flee the moment you're afraid; the sutta's approach is to hold your current posture and watch fear, as a phenomenon that comes and goes, withdraw on its own. Third, cultivate mindfulness and concentration in daily life so the mind is already steady and fear has less to cling to.

faq.q: When fear comes, should I change posture or get up and move around?
faq.a: MN 4's answer is counterintuitive: don't change. The Buddha says that when fear came while he was walking, he kept walking—not standing, sitting, or lying down—until he had dispelled it; and the same when it came while standing, sitting, or lying. In every case he received fear in the very posture it caught him in, never changing position or fleeing because he was afraid. The point is not to let fear command the body—the instinct when afraid is to move and to flee, and he deliberately denies fear that satisfaction, letting it withdraw while he stays still.

faq.q: Did the Buddha himself feel fear?
faq.a: In MN 4 the Buddha admits that before his awakening, while still a bodhisatta, he too found forest lodgings hard to bear and felt that the forests seemed to carry off the mind. He does not portray himself as fearless by nature but describes a process of deliberately facing and gradually overcoming fear. The sutta also holds that fear is largely invited by the practitioner's own timidity, restlessness, doubt, and the like; only after examining each item and confirming he was free of these defilements did he dwell all the more at ease in the forest. Facing fear is thus both a skill in the moment and the fruit of long-term inner purification.
